analysis.one_liner: Expands automatic, online, and same-day voter registration and requires early voting and mail ballots nationwide.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 24, 2021 with one cosponsor, it was sent to the Senate Rules Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten federal election rules to make registering and voting easier: every state would have to offer online voter registration, register eligible people automatically unless they opt out, allow same-day registration at the polls, provide at least two weeks of early voting, and let anyone vote by mail without extra conditions. It also would restrict how states remove voters from the rolls, ban the challenge practice known as voter caging, restore federal voting rights to people who finish a felony sentence, require secure ballot drop boxes, and permanently fund the federal Election Assistance Commission with $500 million in grants to help states comply [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters — especially people with disabilities, hourly workers who cannot take time off on a single election day, frequent movers, students, people recently released from prison, and military and overseas voters — who would find it easier to register and cast a ballot. States also gain grant funding to modernize their registration systems [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, especially disabled, low-income, and mobile voters

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state to offer online voter registration, automatic registration through agencies like motor vehicle offices, Medicaid, and colleges, and same-day registration at the polls [S2] [S3].
Requires states to offer early voting and no-excuse voting by mail, plus secured drop boxes for absentee ballots [S2].
Limits removing voters from the rolls, bans voter caging, and prohibits interfering with voter registration or voting [S2].
Restores the federal right to vote to citizens who have completed a felony sentence, and expands absentee registration and voting for people with disabilities [S2].
Authorizes $500 million in Election Assistance Commission grants to help states build automatic and online registration systems, and permanently reauthorizes the EAC [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: States and their taxpayers bear the cost of building and running online, automatic, and same-day registration systems and drop boxes, offset by the federal grants; anyone opposed to uniform federal election rules also sees state control over election procedures narrowed [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: State election budgets and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Automatic registration moves personal data from many government agencies into state voter files, which is why the bill itself requires the National Institute of Standards and Technology to write new privacy and data-matching standards and bars using registration data for commercial purposes [S3].

Online registration and electronic signature transfer create cybersecurity exposure; the bill responds by requiring states to adopt technological security measures and NIST security standards before receiving grant money [S3].

Preempts state election procedures with federal mandates, which states and officials who favor local control of elections opposed in principle during this period; the bill partially accommodates this by exempting states that already run their own automatic registration systems [S3].
The federal grants and ongoing compliance costs add to federal and state election spending, with $500 million authorized for the first year and open-ended sums thereafter [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For eligible voters the bill is a clear expansion of access: registration becomes nearly automatic and voting windows widen from a single day to weeks. The real costs are money and administrative work — states must integrate agency data, secure their systems, and run longer voting periods — and a real transfer of election rulemaking from states to the federal government. The privacy and security risks are real but addressed directly in the bill's own standards requirements. The largest honest objection is the federalism one, not a design flaw.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill, joined by Senator Raphael Warnock, on March 24, 2021 [S1] [S3] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration the same day [S5].
That was the only action ever taken: no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S1] [S5].
One additional Democratic senator cosponsored, making two supporters in total in the Senate [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State election systems stay as they are: no state had to change its registration, early voting, or mail ballot rules, and officials preferring state control of election procedures were spared a federal mandate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State election officials and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Voter Empowerment Act of 2021 in the Senate on March 24, 2021.

for.name: Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Joined Gillibrand in introducing the bill, as recorded on the bill's face.

for.name: 1 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional Senate supporter it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on March 24, 2021 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: Uniformly opposed the broader 2021 federal voting-rights package this bill overlapped with, keeping similar election overhaul bills from reaching the floor; this bill, with two supporters, never came close to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All known support came from two Democrats and the sole cosponsor was a Democrat; Republicans offered no sponsorship, and no votes were ever taken to break down by party [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill authorizes $500 million in grants and ongoing sums for states to build online and automatic registration systems, electronic signature transfer, and updated registration websites — work that flows to election software and technology providers [S3]. Its outcome is a public benefit (easier registration) and a vendor gain at the same time.

A larger, easier-to-reach electorate changes who turns out, which helps whichever party benefits from higher participation and hurts the other; the bill keeps registration data available for political purposes while barring commercial use [S3].

The bill imposes major new federal mandates on state election offices — automatic registration, early voting, mail voting, drop boxes — while funding them with federal grants and exempting states that already run their own systems [S3].
